bw: Medullary center that controls vessel tone
tp: Changes in vessel diameter alter peripheral resistance, pressure and flow, and therefore cardiac output.

ww.Cardioaccelerator centers: These speed the heart through the cardiac accelerator nerve.
ww.Cardioinhibitor centers: These slow the heart through the vagus nerve.

evidence: The vasomotor centers control vessel tone or contraction of the smooth muscle in the tunica media.

bw: Baroreceptors fire at a higher rate
tp: Cardiac output falls and sympathetic input to the arterioles decreases, causing vasodilation, so blood pressure falls.

ww.Sympathetic stimulation: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart rises when blood pressure drops too low.
ww.Increased ADH release: ADH is triggered by increased osmolarity, not by the baroreceptor reflex for high pressure.

evidence: When blood pressure rises too high, the baroreceptors fire at a higher rate and trigger parasympathetic stimulation of the heart.

tp: Sympathetic stimulation of the peripheral vessels also causes vasoconstriction, so blood pressure rises.

ww.Parasympathetic stimulation: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart rises when pressure is too high.
ww.Vagal discharge: The vagus is the parasympathetic nerve and slows the heart.

evidence: This will trigger an increase in sympathetic stimulation of the heart, causing cardiac output to increase.

bw: Chemoreceptors for O2, CO2 and pH
tp: Chemoreceptors signal both the cardiovascular center and the respiratory centers of the medulla.

ww.Venae cavae and right atrium: Low-pressure baroreceptors, not these chemoreceptors, are found there.
ww.Renal arterioles: The source places these chemoreceptors by the aortic and carotid baroreceptors.

evidence: Chemoreceptors monitoring the blood are located in close proximity to the baroreceptors in the aortic and carotid sinuses.

tp: Falling CO2 and rising pH do the opposite: cardioinhibitor centers are stimulated and vessels dilate.

ww.Less output, dilated vessels: That is the response to falling CO2 and rising pH.
ww.More output, dilated vessels: The vasomotor center is stimulated, so vessels constrict.

evidence: The chemoreceptors respond to increasing carbon dioxide and hydrogen ion levels (falling pH) by stimulating the cardioaccelerator and vasomotor centers, increasing cardiac output and constricting peripheral vessels.

tp: ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb more water and also constricts peripheral vessels.

ww.Falling plasma sodium: That would lower osmolarity and suppress ADH.
ww.Rising blood pressure: High pressure would not call for conserving more water.

evidence: The primary trigger prompting the hypothalamus to release ADH is increasing osmolarity of tissue fluid, usually in response to significant loss of blood volume.

bw: Secrete renin when blood pressure falls
tp: Renin converts liver-made angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

ww.Podocytes: Podocytes are filtration cells of the glomerulus.
ww.Chromaffin cells: Chromaffin cells are in the adrenal medulla.

evidence: Specialized cells in the kidneys , called juxtaglomerular (JG) cells, respond to decreased blood pressure by secreting renin into the blood.

tp: Angiotensin II also stimulates the thirst center in the hypothalamus, so fluid intake rises.

ww.Angiotensin I: Angiotensin I is the precursor and is converted to angiotensin II in the lungs.
ww.Atrial natriuretic hormone: ANH is an antagonist of angiotensin II and lowers blood pressure.

evidence: Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor, greatly increasing blood pressure.

tp: Aldosterone is produced by the adrenal cortex.

ww.Blood volume and pressure fall: Retaining sodium and water does the opposite.

evidence: This in turn increases blood volume, raising blood pressure.

bw: Released by the kidneys when blood flow or oxygen falls
tp: EPO is also a vasoconstrictor. Overproduction raises viscosity, resistance and pressure and lowers flow.

ww.Renin: Renin is an enzyme from JG cells in the RAAS.
ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex hormone that retains sodium.

evidence: Erythropoietin (EPO) is released by the kidneys when blood flow and/or oxygen levels decrease.

bw: Secreted by atrial cells stretched by high blood volume
Promotes loss of sodium and water
tp: B-type natriuretic hormone from the ventricles has similar effects. Both suppress renin, aldosterone and ADH.

ww.Antidiuretic hormone (ADH): ADH retains water, the opposite effect.

evidence: Secreted by cells in the atria of the heart, atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH) (also known as atrial natriuretic peptide) is secreted when blood volume is high enough to cause extreme stretching of the cardiac cells.

bw: Effect on blood volume and pressure
tp: They promote loss of sodium and water from the kidneys.

ww.Both rise: Natriuretic hormones promote loss of fluid.

evidence: All of these actions promote loss of fluid from the body, so blood volume and blood pressure drop.

bw: Endothelial cells release this powerful vasodilator
Triggered by low O2, high CO2 and lactic acid
tp: Opening of the precapillary sphincter also follows rising potassium, falling pH, histamine and warmth.

ww.Norepinephrine: Norepinephrine from sympathetic neurons mostly constricts vessels.

evidence: These conditions in turn stimulate the release of NO, a powerful vasodilator, from endothelial cells (see Figure 20.17).

tp: Platelet secretions and certain prostaglandins may also trigger constriction of the precapillary sphincter.

ww.Histamine: Inflammatory chemicals such as histamine open the sphincters.

evidence: Contraction of the precapillary sphincter is triggered by the opposite levels of the regulators, which prompt the release of endothelins, powerful vasoconstricting peptides secreted by endothelial cells.

bw: Arteriole smooth muscle reacts to being stretched
tp: Low flow relaxes the smooth muscle (dilation); high flow contracts it (constriction).

ww.Baroreceptor reflex: This is a neural reflex through the cardiovascular center, not a purely local response.
ww.Atrial reflex: This is a neural reflex from the right atrium.

evidence: The myogenic response is a reaction to the stretching of the smooth muscle in the walls of arterioles as changes in blood flow occur through the vessel.

bw: Blood flow is nearly constant at rest and exercise
tp: Brain vessels largely do not respond to regulatory stimuli because they lack the appropriate receptors.

ww.Skeletal muscle: Muscle flow rises from 1200 to 12,500 mL/min with maximal exercise.

evidence: Only the brain receives a more or less constant supply of blood whether you are active, resting, thinking, or engaged in any other activity.

tp: Vasodilation occurs in skeletal muscle, heart, lungs, liver and skin.

ww.Skin and lungs: These vessels also dilate during exercise.

evidence: Simultaneously, vasoconstriction occurs in the vessels leading to the kidneys and most of the digestive and reproductive organs.

bw: Skin blood flow rises during exercise
d: To deliver more oxygen to skin
tp: Skin (integument) flow rises from 500 to 1900 mL/min at maximal exercise.

ww.To deliver more oxygen to skin: The source gives heat loss as the reason.
ww.To raise blood pressure: Diverting blood to the skin does not raise pressure.

evidence: During exercise, the body distributes more blood to the body surface where it can dissipate the excess heat generated by increased activity into the environment.

bw: Delivers the same blood as a nonathlete
ans: Higher stroke volume, lower heart rate
d: Lower stroke volume, higher heart rate
Same stroke volume, higher heart rate
tp: The efficiency lets an athlete exercise longer and puts less stress on the heart.

ww.Lower stroke volume, higher heart rate: A larger heart ejects more per beat.
ww.Same stroke volume, higher heart rate: A larger heart increases stroke volume.

evidence: Because an athlete’s heart is larger than a nonathlete’s, stroke volume increases, so the athletic heart can deliver the same amount of blood as the nonathletic heart but with a lower heart rate.

tp: The 2017 guidelines list hypertension that should be treated as 130/80 mm Hg.

ww.Below 140/90 mm Hg: This is above the 2017 threshold for normal.
ww.Below 130/80 mm Hg: This is the treatment threshold for hypertension in the 2017 guideline, not normal.

evidence: New guidelines in 2017 from the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association list normal blood pressure (BP) as less than 120/80 mm Hg and elevated BP as systolic P between 120–129 and diastolic P less than 80 mm Hg.

bw: Ballooning of a vessel from a weakened wall
tp: Hypertension is typically silent and may also lead to peripheral arterial disease, chronic kidney disease and heart failure.

ww.Atherosclerosis: This is plaque buildup in the wall, not ballooning.
ww.Embolism: An embolus is a traveling clot or plaque fragment.

evidence: Hypertension may also lead to an aneurysm (ballooning of a blood vessel caused by a weakening of the wall), peripheral arterial disease (obstruction of vessels in peripheral regions of the body), chronic kidney disease, or heart failure.

bw: Heart rate rises to restore cardiac output
tp: Vasoconstriction of arterioles raises resistance and constriction of veins raises venous return.

ww.About 100–120 beats per minute: The source puts the response higher, at 180–200.
ww.About 60–80 beats per minute: A rate this low would not restore output after blood loss.

evidence: This typically prompts the heart rate to increase to about 180–200 contractions per minute, restoring cardiac output to normal levels.

bw: Blood loss compensated by sympathetic responses
Usually restores normal pressure if loss is below this
tp: Restoring the lost volume needs the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone mechanism, thirst and EPO.

ww.50 percent of blood volume: The source threshold is 20 percent; losing much more is life threatening.

evidence: If blood loss were less than 20 percent of total blood volume, these responses together would usually return blood pressure to normal and redirect the remaining blood to the tissues.

bw: Shock from hemorrhage, burns or vomiting
Thready pulse and cool clammy skin
tp: Treatment is IV fluids and drugs such as dopamine, epinephrine and norepinephrine to raise blood pressure.

ww.Cardiogenic shock: Cardiogenic shock is failure of the heart to maintain output.
ww.Septic shock: Septic shock is vascular shock from widespread infection.

evidence: Hypovolemic shock in adults is typically caused by hemorrhage, although in children it may be caused by fluid losses related to severe vomiting or diarrhea.

bw: Most often after a myocardial infarction
tp: Treatment fixes the damage to the heart or its vessels rather than treating the shock directly.

ww.Hypovolemic shock: Hypovolemic shock is due to volume loss.
ww.Anaphylactic shock: Anaphylactic shock is a vascular shock from histamine release.

evidence: Cardiogenic shock results from the inability of the heart to maintain cardiac output.

tp: It is a form of vascular shock, where arterioles lose tone and dilate dramatically.

ww.Neurogenic shock: Neurogenic shock follows cranial or spinal injury that damages the medullary cardiovascular centers.
ww.Cardiogenic shock: Cardiogenic shock is a failure of the heart to maintain output.

evidence: Anaphylactic shock is a severe allergic response that causes the widespread release of histamines, triggering vasodilation throughout the body.

tp: Neurogenic shock is a type of vascular shock.

ww.Anaphylactic shock: Anaphylactic shock is caused by an allergic reaction.
ww.Hypovolemic shock: Hypovolemic shock is caused by loss of volume.

evidence: Neurogenic shock is a form of vascular shock that occurs with cranial or spinal injuries that damage the cardiovascular centers in the medulla oblongata or the nervous fibers originating from this region.

tp: Sepsis, or septicemia, is also called blood poisoning. Treatment includes fluids, pressor agents and removing the cause.

ww.Cardiogenic shock: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure of the heart.

evidence: A common cause is sepsis (or septicemia), also called “blood poisoning,” which is a widespread bacterial infection that results in an organismal-level inflammatory response known as septic shock.

bw: Significant portion of the vascular system blocked
Pulmonary embolism is the most common cause
tp: Treatment depends on the cause and may include anticoagulants, draining pericardial fluid or air, or surgery.

ww.Hypovolemic shock: Hypovolemic shock is loss of volume rather than blockage.
ww.Septic shock: Septic shock is vasodilation from infection.

evidence: Obstructive shock, as the name would suggest, occurs when a significant portion of the vascular system is blocked.

bw: Excess fluid in the pericardial cavity
Heart cannot fully relax and fill
tp: Tamponade is one cause of obstructive shock; treatment removes fluid from the pericardial cavity.

ww.Pneumothorax: Pneumothorax is excess air in the thoracic cavity outside the lungs.
ww.Aortic valve stenosis: Stenosis is a narrowed valve that obstructs outflow.

evidence: Other causes include stenosis of the aortic valve; cardiac tamponade, in which excess fluid in the pericardial cavity interferes with the ability of the heart to fully relax and fill with blood (resulting in decreased preload); and a pneumothorax, in which an excessive amount of air is present in the thoracic cavity, outside of the lungs, which interferes with venous return, pulmonary function, and delivery of oxygen to the tissues.

bw: Behaves like this type of loop
tp: If uncorrected, shock may lead to the death of the patient.

ww.Negative-feedback loop: A negative loop would restore balance.
ww.Feed-forward loop: The source describes shock as a positive-feedback loop.

evidence: Unfortunately, shock is an example of a positive-feedback loop that, if uncorrected, may lead to the death of the patient.
